title: What If Everyone Could See Your Salary? #shorts
note: scene Short (src/v6/SalShort.tsx) — salary-over-heads street; plan from pipeline/scenes/sal1.json
sources: S1 Perez-Truglia, 'The Effects of Income Transparency on Well-Being: Evidence from a Natural Experiment' (AER 2020 / NBER w25622): in fall 2001 Norwegian media put tax records online so anyone could search anyone's income — before that you had to ask in person at the tax office https://www.nber.org/papers/w25622

S2 same paper: higher transparency increased the happiness gap between richer and poorer individuals by 29% (life-satisfaction gap +21%); poorer people became less happy, richer more happy, with no change in income https://www.nber.org/papers/w25622

S3 Reuters (Doyle/Scrutton) via Investing.com + BBC 'Norway: the country where no salaries are secret' (2017): searches stopped being anonymous in 2014 — the person searched can see the searcher's name; lookups fell from 16.5 million in the 12 months to Oct 2014 to 2.15 million https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/40669239
S4 Statistics Norway: population ~5.1 million in 2014 https://www.ssb.no/en/befolkning

beats.text: What if everyone on your street could see your salary?
Because in Norway they actually can.
You type any name into your phone and their income just pops up.
So people looked up their boss and their neighbor and even their ex
sixteen million times in one year in a country of five million people.
But then scientists measured how happy everyone was
and nobody's paycheck changed yet the rich got happier and the poor got sadder.
So Norway changed one tiny rule.
Now when you look someone up they can see your name.
And the searches crashed from sixteen million to two million.
Because people never wanted to know the number.
They just wanted to look without getting caught.
So next time you wonder what your neighbor makes just ask yourself
